question: On 12 December 2023, Hungary introduced a law to protect national sovereignty. It provides for the establishment of a special competent body to monitor, assess and combat possible interference by foreign actors in national elections. That body would be vested with overriding powers, allowing no form of appeal against decisions of the Office for the Defence of Sovereignty.
Several civil society organisations, as well as the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights, fear that this law poses a ‘risk to human rights’. Accordingly: 1.
Is the Commission aware of this legislation and, if so, how does it assess its potential impact on freedom of expression, freedom of the press and freedom of association in Hungary?
Does this law violate EU law and, if it does, what action can the Commission take?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.4.2024) The Act LXXXVIII of 2023 on the Defence of National Sovereignty raises several serious concerns as regards its compliance with EU law.

Following a thorough assessment of this legislative text, adopted by the Hungarian National Assembly in December 2023, in conjunction with the Hungarian Act XXXIII of 1989 on the Operation and Financial Management of Political Parties, and after an exchange of letters at political level, on 7 February 2024 the Commission decided to open an infringement procedure by sending a letter of formal notice to Hungary for violations of EU law1.

The Commission considers that the Hungarian legislation at stake violates several provisions of primary and secondary EU law, among others the democratic values of the EU; the principle of democracy and the electoral rights of EU citizens; several fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, such as the right to respect for private and family life, the right to protection of personal data, the freedom of expression and information, the freedom of association, the electoral rights of EU citizens, the right to an effective remedy and to a fair trial, the privilege against self-incrimination and the legal professional privilege; the requirements of EU law relating to data protection and several rules applicable to the internal market.

Hungary has two months to reply to the letter of formal notice. If it does not address the grievances identified by the Commission, the Commission may decide to send a reasoned opinion as the next step in the infringement procedure.
